hypotheses.claim: Crowd membership can shift behavior through shared norms and identity.
Anonymity and immersion reliably dissolve self-control and produce irrational violence.
Crowds form a single suggestible collective mind manipulated by leaders.
Organized communication can shape attention, interpretation, and behavior.
Modern mass democracy depends on elite management of public opinion.
A small expert group can predictably engineer consent across domains.
People rely on mediated pictures and stereotypes for distant public affairs.
Media attention materially affects which issues audiences consider important.
Ordinary citizens are generally incapable of competent democratic judgment.
Status threat, grievance, and identity needs can increase attraction to mass movements.
Mass movements share recurring organizational and psychological mechanisms.
The frustrated individual is the primary cause of revolutionary, nationalist, and religious mobilization.
Stable authoritarian dispositions predict prejudice and punitive outgroup attitudes.
Submission and dominance are distinct but related pathways to generalized prejudice.
A psychoanalytic family-development account explains fascistic potential across populations.
Situational features substantially change harmful compliance with authority.
Milgram's variations reveal systematic resistance as well as obedience.
Participants delivered shocks through a general agentic-state loss of moral agency.
Aggression has evolutionary and biological components.
Aggression is a unitary hydraulic instinct discharged by innate releasing mechanisms.
Human war follows directly from animal territorial aggression.
Categorization and social learning contribute to prejudice.
Equal-status cooperative intergroup contact can reduce prejudice under supportive conditions.
Contact by itself generally reduces prejudice regardless of status, goals, or institutions.
People strategically manage impressions across social settings.
Roles, audiences, and settings structure which selves are presented.
Most social interaction is best understood as conscious theatrical deception.
Institutions and categories are sustained through repeated social practice and legitimation.
Language and socialization shape experienced reality and taken-for-granted knowledge.
Physical or biological constraints contribute little to social reality.
